value.overview: The Brown Jay (Cyanocorax morio) is a large, noisy, social jay of Central America and southern Texas. It is a familiar bird of forest edges, woodland, gardens, farms, and other partly open habitats. Brown Jays often travel in groups and are known for cooperative breeding, in which nonbreeding birds may help raise young. In Costa Rica, the species is widespread and resident, occurring on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes and in the Central Valley.
value.classification: The Brown Jay belongs to the jay and crow family, Corvidae, and the order Passeriformes. It is placed in the genus Cyanocorax.
value.identification: Adults are large jays with mostly rich brown plumage, a darker brown to nearly black head, and a contrasting pale or whitish throat and upper breast. The wings and tail are dark, often showing a subtle bluish sheen. The bill and legs are black. Brown Jays have a long tail and a strong, heavy bill. Juveniles may have a paler bill and less sharply contrasting head and throat plumage. Their loud, varied calls are often the first clue to their presence.
value.rangeHabitat: The Brown Jay ranges from southern Texas and eastern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, found on both slopes from lowlands into the foothills and commonly up to about 1,500 meters, though it can occur locally higher. It uses humid and seasonally dry forest, forest edges, second growth, plantations, pastures with trees, gardens, and wooded areas near streams. It is also regular around settlements and bird feeders.
value.migrationStatus: The Brown Jay is generally nonmigratory. In Costa Rica it occurs year-round rather than as a seasonal migrant, although local movements may follow food availability, rainfall, or changes in habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Brown Jays breed cooperatively in social groups. More than one bird may help build a nest, and nonbreeding group members can assist with nestling care and feeding. Groups may contain one breeding female or, occasionally, several females with separate nests. The nest is built in vegetation, and the usual clutch is about three to six eggs. Incubation lasts roughly 18 to 20 days, with females performing most incubation while other group members may help defend the territory and provision the young.
value.dietFeeding: The Brown Jay is an opportunistic omnivore. Its diet includes insects and other invertebrates, fruit, seeds, nectar, lizards, frogs, and other small animal prey. It forages in trees and shrubs, searches leaf litter and the ground, and may investigate gardens, farms, picnic areas, and feeding stations. In Costa Rica, it readily uses human-modified habitats where trees, dense cover, and reliable food are available.
value.behavior: Brown Jays are highly social and usually occur in pairs or family groups, sometimes forming larger flocks. They are active, conspicuous, and vocal, using a wide range of harsh calls, whistles, and chatter to maintain contact and defend a territory. Groups cooperate in territorial defense, feeding, and raising young. They commonly move through vegetation by hopping and climbing, but also fly between trees and may boldly approach people or feeding stations.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable.
